summary: This memo defines a mechanism that lets feed publishers express threaded discussions within the Atom Syndication Format, so that an entry can be marked as a reply to another entry.

eli5.summary: Imagine comments on a blog where each reply points to the comment it answers. This adds that reply link to Atom feeds so readers can follow conversations.

questions: how to do threaded replies in atom feeds
how to link replies in an atom feed
what is the replies link relation
subtitle: Extra Atom feed elements that let an entry say which entry it answers and where its replies live.

tldr.problem: The Atom Syndication Format has no standard way to say that one entry is a response to another, so threaded discussions cannot be expressed in a feed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds an in-reply-to element that points to the parent, a replies link relation that points to where responses are found, and optional count, updated and total hints.
tldr.outcome: Feed publishers can express threaded conversations, though the count and date values are advisory and consumers may ignore the extensions.

facts.label: Default type of a replies link

today: RFC 4685 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2006, and no RFC in the unit metadata obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Conventions
sections.content:
RFC 4685 defines an extension for expressing threaded discussions within the Atom Syndication Format (RFC 4287). All the new elements and attributes live in one XML namespace, http://purl.org/syndication/thread/1.0, shown with the prefix thr:. The prefix itself is arbitrary.

The text allows IRIs (RFC 3987) wherever a URI is named. An IRI used for dereferencing MUST be mapped to a URI, while an IRI serving as an identifier MUST NOT be mapped. The schemas shown are non-normative RELAX NG Compact; the prose is the only definition of conformance.
sections.eli5: This is a small add-on to an existing feed language, with its own label so nobody mixes up the new words with the old ones.

sections.title: The in-reply-to Element
sections.content:
The thr:in-reply-to element says that an entry is a response to another resource. It MUST contain a ref attribute: the persistent, universally unique identifier of the resource being answered, built and compared by the same rules as atom:id. Processors MUST NOT assume it can be dereferenced.

Optional attributes add detail. href is an IRI from which a representation of the parent can be retrieved. source is an IRI of an Atom feed or entry document that contains the parent. type hints at the media type of the href target and only matters if href is present. Both href and source, once mapped to URIs, MUST be dereferenceable.

The element is similar to the email in-reply-to header (RFC 2822), but it names exactly one parent. An entry that answers several resources MAY carry several elements, and their order has no meaning. Publishers are advised to add a related link too, so processors that do not know the extension still see a relationship.
sections.eli5: It is like writing "this is my answer to that message" on a note and attaching the message's name tag, so everyone knows which message you mean.

sections.title: The replies Link and the total Element
sections.content:
An Atom link with rel set to replies points to a resource where responses can be found. If type is omitted it is assumed to be application/atom+xml. As a child of a feed or source, it means the target likely holds replies to any of the feed's entries. As a child of an entry, the replies are likely specific to that entry.

Such a link MAY carry thr:count, an unsigned non-negative integer hinting at the number of replies, and thr:updated, an RFC 3339 date-time hinting at the most recent reply. Both are advisory. A feed, entry or source may hold any number of replies links, and processors MUST process each one independently, without assuming they are alternate views of the same resource.

Separately, an entry MAY contain one thr:total element, a non-negative integer for the total number of unique responses the publisher knows of. It MUST NOT appear more than once, and it has no implied relationship to any thr:count value.
sections.eli5: A replies link says "the answers are over there", and the count is a rough guess of how many, like a sign saying "about 10 comments".

sections.title: Using the Count, Updated and Total Hints
sections.content:
The three metadata values let a consumer show basic thread information without fetching and parsing the linked resources. The RFC lists caveats. They MUST NOT be assumed accurate, because the real number of replies MAY differ, though publishers SHOULD try to keep them right.

The values change faster than the entry that holds them, so frequent updates can hurt cacheability and increase bandwidth use. Publishers SHOULD treat a change to them as an insignificant update in the sense of RFC 4287, meaning the container's atom:updated SHOULD NOT change.

Finally, Atom only requires implementations to ignore extensions they do not understand, so some consumers MAY NOT use these extensions at all.
sections.eli5: The numbers are just helpful hints, like a guess at how long a queue is. They can be a little out of date, so do not treat them as exact.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension inherits the security considerations of RFC 4287. A crafted feed could make a consumer start excessive or even unending sequences of network requests, which is a denial-of-service risk. Consumers can ask for user intervention after a number of requests, or apply a hard limit or heuristics.

Because threads can span domains, an attacker could use distributed responses to attach unwanted content to a discussion. Users can be allowed to configure which sources may supply responses, or heuristics can judge legitimacy.

Publishers can also edit what they previously published, and with distributed comments this is harder to detect than in a closed comment system, raising attribution and repudiation concerns. XML Digital Signatures may help, though a valid signature alone is not a reliable defense.
sections.eli5: Anyone can say their post answers yours, even someone you do not trust. So readers should be careful about whose replies they show and not follow links forever.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The specification defines one new Atom link relation type, replies, registered in the IANA Registry of Link Relation. The registration points back to Section 4 of the RFC for its description.
sections.eli5: The new word "replies" was written into the official list of link words so nobody else uses it for something different.

viz.caption: AN ENTRY ANSWERING ANOTHER (EXCERPT OF RFC 4685 EXAMPLE)

data.title: thr:in-reply-to
data.code:
<entry>
  <id>tag:example.org,2005:1,1</id>
  <title>A response to the original</title>
  <updated>2006-03-01T12:12:12Z</updated>
  <link href="http://www.example.org/entries/1/1" />
  <thr:in-reply-to
    ref="tag:example.org,2005:1"
    type="application/xhtml+xml"
    href="http://www.example.org/entries/1"/>
  <summary>This is a response to the original entry</summary>
</entry>

items.title: thr:in-reply-to
items.text: Names the parent of an entry through a required ref attribute.

items.title: replies link
items.text: Points to a resource that likely holds responses.

items.title: thr:count
items.text: Advisory number of replies in the linked resource.

items.title: thr:updated
items.text: Advisory time of the newest reply.

items.title: thr:total
items.text: At most one per entry; total unique responses the publisher knows.
